chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death), is he from the one-third [of the estate]? He said: Yes. And the testator has the right to return [revoke or alter] in his will, whether he be in health or in sickness.

key_terms.الثُّلُث: The third: The portion of the estate that can be bequeathed to non-heirs
key_terms.المُدَبَّر: Mudabbir: A slave whose manumission is contingent upon the owner's death
key_terms.المُوصِي: The testator: The person making the will/bequest
key_terms.صِحَّة: Health: The state of being healthy, as opposed to deathbed
key_terms.مَرَض: Sickness: The state of being ill, often implying the final illness before death

ai.seo_question: Is a Mudabbir included in the one-third share of the estate for bequests in Shia inheritance law?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a *Mudabbir* (a slave promised freedom upon the owner's death) is counted within the one-third share of the estate that can be bequeathed to non-heirs, a key distinction in Shia jurisprudence regarding inheritance distribution. The Imam further establishes the principle of *khiyar* (optionality), confirming that the owner retains the right to revoke or modify this specific bequest at any time, whether in good health or during illness, emphasizing the flexibility of testamentary disposition before death.
